interactionPlan.concept: The relationship between model complexity (polynomial order K), training approximation error, and generalization error, highlighting the phenomena of underfitting and overfitting.
learningObjectives: After engaging with this figure, the student will understand why training (approximation) error continuously decreases with model complexity while validation (generalization) error is U-shaped.
The student will be able to visually identify the zones of underfitting, optimal fitting, and overfitting on an error-vs-complexity plot.
The student will be able to explain why minimizing training error to zero often results in poor performance on unseen data.
interactionPlan.keyInsight: The lowest training error does not mean the best model; beyond a certain complexity, a model starts memorizing noise, causing training error to drop to zero while generalization error skyrockets.

interactions.label: Polynomial Degree (K)
interactions.effect: Moves a vertical locator bar across the plot, highlighting the precise values of 'approx' and 'gen' error for the selected model complexity. It also dynamically displays a mini-plot showing how a polynomial of degree K fits a set of sample data points.
interactions.teaches: How changing model capacity directly impacts the trade-off between fitting training data and generalizing to validation data.

interactions.label: Show Regimes
interactions.effect: Overlays shaded vertical bands on the plot representing three regimes: Underfitting (K < 3), Optimal Fit (K = 3), and Overfitting (K > 3).
interactions.teaches: The boundary thresholds between underfitting, optimal complexity, and overfitting.

demo_steps.title: When Models are Too Simple
demo_steps.narration: Start by looking at the far left where the polynomial degree K is 0, 1, or 2. Notice that both the solid line ('approx' training error) and the dashed line ('gen' validation error) are near maximum error. This is 'underfitting'—the model lacks the capacity to capture the underlying pattern in the data, resulting in poor performance on both training and validation sets.
demo_steps.focus: The high error plateau on both curves in the shaded 'Underfitting' region (K = 0 to 2).

demo_steps.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
demo_steps.narration: Now, slide the degree K to 3. Notice that the dashed validation error ('gen') drops dramatically to its lowest point, while the training error ('approx') also falls. This is the optimal model complexity, where the model has learned the true underlying physical process without fitting to the random noise.
demo_steps.focus: The local minimum of the dashed 'gen' curve at K = 3.

demo_steps.title: The Overfitting Divergence
demo_steps.narration: Move K higher, up to 6 or 8. Watch what happens: the solid line ('approx') plummets to zero, meaning it perfectly predicts every training point. However, the dashed line ('gen') starts climbing back up. This divergence is 'overfitting'—the high-degree model is using its extra capacity to pass perfectly through noisy training points, which ruins its predictions on unseen test queries.
demo_steps.focus: The widening gap between the plummeting solid curve and the rising dashed curve for K > 3.

demo_steps.title: The Golden Rule of ML
demo_steps.narration: Compare the end points of both curves. If you only looked at training error, you would mistakenly conclude that K = 9 is the best model because its error is zero. But looking at validation error proves it is actually one of the worst. Always evaluate models on validation data to ensure you are at the bottom of the generalization U-curve.
demo_steps.focus: The stark contrast at K = 9 where approximation error is 0.0 but generalization error is near 0.85.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: A line plot with two curves. The X-axis ranges from 0 to 9 (integer steps representing K). The Y-axis represents 'Error' ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. The solid black curve labeled 'approx' starts at 1.0 (for K=0..2), drops sharply to ~0.22 at K=3, rises slightly to ~0.33 at K=4, then decreases to 0.0 by K=6 and stays flat at 0.0. The dashed black curve labeled 'gen' starts at ~0.95 (for K=0..2), drops to its minimum of ~0.52 at K=3, and then steadily climbs back up, ending around 0.85 at K=9. Labels 'approx' and 'gen' should sit clearly near the right end of their respective curves. Shaded background zones (red for underfitting K<3, green vertical slice for K=3, orange/red for overfitting K>3) should appear when the region toggle is active.
